title: FizzBuzz
question: Implement `func FizzBuzz(n int) []string`. Return a slice of length n where index i (1-based value i+1) is "Fizz" if divisible by 3, "Buzz" if divisible by 5, "FizzBuzz" if divisible by both, otherwise the number as a string.
solutionCode:
package main

import "strconv"

func FizzBuzz(n int) []string {
	out := make([]string, 0, n)              // preallocate capacity n to avoid repeated regrowth
	for i := 1; i <= n; i++ {                // iterate over the values 1..n inclusive
		switch {                             // tagless switch acts like an if/else chain
		case i%15 == 0:                      // divisible by both 3 and 5
			out = append(out, "FizzBuzz")
		case i%3 == 0:                       // divisible by 3 only
			out = append(out, "Fizz")
		case i%5 == 0:                       // divisible by 5 only
			out = append(out, "Buzz")
		default:                             // otherwise emit the number itself
			out = append(out, strconv.Itoa(i)) // convert the int to its decimal string
		}
	}
	return out                               // the assembled FizzBuzz slice
}

hint:

3. Otherwise convert the number with strconv.Itoa.

strconv.Itoa is the idiomatic int-to-string conversion; string(i) would produce a rune, not a number.

optimized: Single loop with a tagless switch, preallocated slice. Time Complexity: O(N).

title: Reverse Integer
question: Implement `func ReverseInt(x int) int` that reverses the digits of a signed 32-bit integer. If the reversed value overflows the int32 range, return 0. The sign must be preserved.
solutionCode:
package main

import "math"

func ReverseInt(x int) int {
	res := 0                                 // accumulated reversed number
	for x != 0 {                             // process each digit until x is exhausted
		digit := x % 10                      // pop the last digit (keeps sign in Go: -123%10 == -3)
		x /= 10                              // drop that digit from x
		res = res*10 + digit                 // shift result left and append the popped digit
		if res > math.MaxInt32 || res < math.MinInt32 { // detect overflow of the signed 32-bit range
			return 0                         // per spec, overflow yields 0
		}
	}
	return res                               // the sign-preserving reversed integer
}
hint:
1. Use %10 and /10 to pop digits.
2. Build the result with res*10 + digit.
3. Check int32 bounds after each step.
constraints: Input fits in int32. Return 0 if the reversed result would overflow int32.
hints: In Go the sign of a%b follows the dividend, so -123 % 10 is -3 — the sign carries naturally.
math.MaxInt32 and math.MinInt32 give clean overflow bounds.
bruteForce: Convert to a string, reverse it, parse back, then range-check. Time Complexity: O(d).
optimized: Arithmetic digit popping with an overflow guard each step. Time Complexity: O(d).

// GroupAnagrams groups words that are anagrams using a sorted-letter signature.
func GroupAnagrams(strs []string) [][]string {
	groups := make(map[string][]string)        // signature -> words sharing that signature
	for _, w := range strs {                   // process each input word in order
		b := []byte(w)                     // copy bytes so we can sort the letters
		sort.Slice(b, func(i, j int) bool { return b[i] < b[j] }) // sort letters into a canonical key
		key := string(b)                   // identical anagrams now share an identical key
		groups[key] = append(groups[key], w) // append the original word to its bucket
	}
	result := make([][]string, 0, len(groups)) // collect buckets into the output
	for _, g := range groups {                 // map order is random, which is acceptable here
		result = append(result, g)         // each bucket is one anagram group
	}
	return result                              // grouped anagrams
}

package main

// ProductExceptSelf computes per-index products of all other elements without division.
func ProductExceptSelf(nums []int) []int {
	n := len(nums)                // length of the input
	res := make([]int, n)         // output slice
	prefix := 1                   // running product of everything to the left of i
	for i := 0; i < n; i++ {      // left-to-right pass fills prefixes
		res[i] = prefix       // res[i] = product of all elements before i
		prefix *= nums[i]     // extend the prefix to include nums[i]
	}
	suffix := 1                   // running product of everything to the right of i
	for i := n - 1; i >= 0; i-- { // right-to-left pass multiplies in suffixes
		res[i] *= suffix      // combine left prefix with right suffix
		suffix *= nums[i]     // extend the suffix to include nums[i]
	}
	return res // each res[i] excludes nums[i]
}

question: Write `func FindKthLargest(nums []int, k int) int` returning the k-th largest element. Use container/heap to maintain a size-k min-heap whose root is the answer after processing all elements.
solutionCode:
package main

import "container/heap" // heap operations on the int min-heap

// intHeap is a min-heap of ints (smallest at the root).
type intHeap []int

func (h intHeap) Len() int           { return len(h) }            // size
func (h intHeap) Less(i, j int) bool { return h[i] < h[j] }       // min-heap ordering
func (h intHeap) Swap(i, j int)      { h[i], h[j] = h[j], h[i] }  // swap
func (h *intHeap) Push(x any)        { *h = append(*h, x.(int)) } // append on push
func (h *intHeap) Pop() any {                                     // pop the last element
	old := *h     // backing slice
	n := len(old) // current length
	v := old[n-1] // element heap placed at the end
	*h = old[:n-1] // shrink
	return v       // return popped value
}

// FindKthLargest keeps the k largest values in a size-k min-heap.
func FindKthLargest(nums []int, k int) int {
	h := &intHeap{}          // empty min-heap
	heap.Init(h)             // initialize heap invariants
	for _, n := range nums { // stream every number
		heap.Push(h, n)  // push the value
		if h.Len() > k { // keep only k elements
			heap.Pop(h) // drop the current smallest
		}
	}
	return (*h)[0] // the heap root is the smallest of the k largest = k-th largest
}
hint:
1. Maintain a min-heap of size k.
2. Push each value; if size exceeds k, pop the smallest.
3. The root is the k-th largest.

title: Course Schedule (topo sort)
question: Write `func canFinish(numCourses int, prerequisites [][]int) bool`. Each pair [a,b] means course a depends on b. Return true if all courses can be completed, i.e. the dependency graph has no cycle. Use Kahn's BFS topological sort.
solutionCode:
package main

func canFinish(numCourses int, prerequisites [][]int) bool {
	adj := make([][]int, numCourses)   // adjacency list: b -> list of dependents a
	indeg := make([]int, numCourses)   // in-degree (number of unmet prerequisites) per course
	for _, p := range prerequisites {  // build the graph from edges
		a, b := p[0], p[1]         // a depends on b, so edge b -> a
		adj[b] = append(adj[b], a) // record the outgoing edge
		indeg[a]++                 // a has one more prerequisite
	}
	queue := make([]int, 0, numCourses) // courses with no remaining prerequisites
	for c := 0; c < numCourses; c++ {   // seed the queue
		if indeg[c] == 0 { // ready to take immediately
			queue = append(queue, c)
		}
	}
	taken := 0           // count of courses we have scheduled
	for len(queue) > 0 { // process in topological order
		c := queue[0]      // pop the front
		queue = queue[1:]  // advance the queue
		taken++            // this course is now completed
		for _, nxt := range adj[c] { // relax each dependent
			indeg[nxt]-- // one prerequisite satisfied
			if indeg[nxt] == 0 { // all prerequisites met
				queue = append(queue, nxt) // it becomes available
			}
		}
	}
	return taken == numCourses // all scheduled means acyclic
}
hint:
1. Build adjacency + in-degree arrays.
2. Start from nodes with in-degree 0.
3. If you can schedule every node, there is no cycle.
constraints: 1 <= numCourses <= 10^5, edges may contain duplicates. O(V+E).
hints: Kahn's algorithm peels off zero-in-degree nodes layer by layer.
If the processed count is below numCourses, a cycle blocked the rest.

title: Subsets (backtracking)
question: Write `func subsets(nums []int) [][]int`. Return all possible subsets (the power set) of the distinct integers. Use backtracking.
solutionCode:
package main

func subsets(nums []int) [][]int {
	res := [][]int{}        // accumulates every subset
	cur := []int{}          // the subset being built
	var backtrack func(start int) // explore choices from index 'start'
	backtrack = func(start int) {
		combo := make([]int, len(cur)) // copy current subset (cur is reused)
		copy(combo, cur)               // snapshot to avoid aliasing
		res = append(res, combo)       // every node in the tree is a valid subset
		for i := start; i < len(nums); i++ { // try adding each later element
			cur = append(cur, nums[i]) // choose nums[i]
			backtrack(i + 1)           // recurse on the remaining elements
			cur = cur[:len(cur)-1]     // undo the choice (backtrack)
		}
	}
	backtrack(0) // start from the first index
	return res   // 2^n subsets
}
hint:
1. Every recursion node is a subset.
2. Add the current subset, then extend with each later element.
3. Pop after recursing.
constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 10, distinct values.
hints: Copy the current slice before storing it, since the buffer is mutated.
Passing a start index prevents generating the same subset twice.
bruteForce: Iterate bitmasks 0..2^n-1 building each subset. Time Complexity: O(n*2^n).
optimized: Backtracking with a shared buffer. Time Complexity: O(n*2^n).

discussion.mistakes: Appending the live cur slice (all entries alias the same backing array).
followUps: Handle duplicates so subsets stay unique.

title: Permutations (backtracking)
question: Write `func permute(nums []int) [][]int`. Return all permutations of the distinct integers. Use backtracking with a used marker.
solutionCode:
package main

func permute(nums []int) [][]int {
	res := [][]int{}                // all permutations
	cur := []int{}                  // permutation under construction
	used := make([]bool, len(nums)) // whether each index is already placed
	var backtrack func()            // build one position at a time
	backtrack = func() {
		if len(cur) == len(nums) { // a full permutation is complete
			perm := make([]int, len(cur)) // copy out the result
			copy(perm, cur)
			res = append(res, perm)
			return
		}
		for i := 0; i < len(nums); i++ { // try every element for this slot
			if used[i] { // skip elements already in the permutation
				continue
			}
			used[i] = true                 // mark chosen
			cur = append(cur, nums[i])     // place it
			backtrack()                    // fill the remaining slots
			cur = cur[:len(cur)-1]         // remove it (undo)
			used[i] = false                // mark available again
		}
	}
	backtrack() // begin recursion
	return res  // n! permutations
}
hint:
1. Track which indices are used.
2. Fill one slot at a time with each unused element.
3. Snapshot when the permutation is full.
constraints: 1 <= len(nums) <= 8, distinct values.
hints: A boolean used slice avoids re-picking the same element.
Always copy cur before appending it to results.
bruteForce: Generate then filter, or use Heap's algorithm. Time Complexity: O(n*n!).
optimized: Backtracking with a used marker. Time Complexity: O(n*n!).

discussion.mistakes: Forgetting to reset used[i] or storing the live cur slice.
followUps: Permute a multiset without duplicate permutations.

title: Generate Parentheses (backtracking)
question: Write `func generateParenthesis(n int) []string`. Return all combinations of n pairs of well-formed parentheses. Backtrack tracking open and close counts.
solutionCode:
package main

func generateParenthesis(n int) []string {
	res := []string{}                       // all valid strings
	buf := make([]byte, 0, 2*n)             // current string being built
	var backtrack func(open, close int)     // open/close counts placed so far
	backtrack = func(open, close int) {
		if len(buf) == 2*n { // used all 2n characters -> complete string
			res = append(res, string(buf)) // snapshot it
			return
		}
		if open < n { // can still open a new pair
			buf = append(buf, '(')      // place '('
			backtrack(open+1, close)    // recurse
			buf = buf[:len(buf)-1]      // undo
		}
		if close < open { // can close only if an unmatched '(' exists
			buf = append(buf, ')')      // place ')'
			backtrack(open, close+1)    // recurse
			buf = buf[:len(buf)-1]      // undo
		}
	}
	backtrack(0, 0) // start empty
	return res      // Catalan(n) valid strings
}
hint:
1. Add '(' while open < n.
2. Add ')' only while close < open.
3. Record when length is 2n.
hints: The close<open rule guarantees the string stays balanced as it grows.
Reusing a byte buffer is cheaper than concatenating strings.
bruteForce: Generate all 2^(2n) sequences and keep the valid ones. Time Complexity: O(2^(2n) * n).
optimized: Backtracking that only builds valid prefixes. Time Complexity: O(4^n / sqrt(n)).

discussion.mistakes: Allowing ')' when close >= open or forgetting to undo the buffer append.
followUps: Count valid strings without generating them (Catalan number).

solutionCode:
package main

func dailyTemperatures(temps []int) []int {
	res := make([]int, len(temps))      // answer[i] = days to wait (default 0)
	stack := make([]int, 0, len(temps)) // indices of days still waiting, temps decreasing
	for i, t := range temps {           // process each day left to right
		for len(stack) > 0 && temps[stack[len(stack)-1]] < t { // current day is warmer than stack top
			prev := stack[len(stack)-1]   // index awaiting a warmer day
			stack = stack[:len(stack)-1]  // resolve and pop it
			res[prev] = i - prev          // distance to the warmer day
		}
		stack = append(stack, i) // current day waits for its own warmer day
	}
	return res // remaining stacked days keep their default 0
}
hint:
1. Keep a stack of indices with decreasing temperatures.
2. When a warmer day arrives, pop and record the gap.
3. Unresolved days stay 0.
constraints: 1 <= len(temps) <= 10^5.

title: Worker Pool (channels + WaitGroup)
question: Write `func sumOfSquares(nums []int, workers int) int`. Distribute the work across a fixed pool of `workers` goroutines that each read jobs from a jobs channel, square the value, and send it to a results channel. Use sync.WaitGroup to know when all workers are done, then aggregate. The result must be deterministic regardless of scheduling.
solutionCode:
package main

import "sync"

func sumOfSquares(nums []int, workers int) int {
	if workers < 1 { // guard against a non-positive pool size
		workers = 1 // fall back to a single worker
	}
	jobs := make(chan int, len(nums))    // buffered queue of input values
	results := make(chan int, len(nums)) // buffered queue of squared values
	var wg sync.WaitGroup                // tracks active workers
	for w := 0; w < workers; w++ {       // launch the fixed worker pool
		wg.Add(1)            // register this worker
		go func() {          // each worker runs concurrently
			defer wg.Done()                  // signal completion on return
			for n := range jobs {            // pull jobs until the channel is closed
				results <- n * n         // compute and emit the square
			}
		}()
	}
	for _, n := range nums { // enqueue every job
		jobs <- n
	}
	close(jobs) // no more jobs; workers will drain and exit
	go func() {         // close results once all workers finish
		wg.Wait()   // block until every worker returned
		close(results) // unblock the aggregation range below
	}()
	sum := 0                    // accumulate squared values
	for r := range results {    // fan in until results is closed
		sum += r // addition is commutative, so order does not matter
	}
	return sum // deterministic total regardless of scheduling
}
hint:
1. Buffer the jobs and results channels.
2. Each worker ranges over jobs and exits when it closes.
3. Close results after wg.Wait, then sum.
constraints: 0 <= len(nums) <= 10^6, 1 <= workers <= 256. Aggregation must be order-independent.
hints: Closing jobs is the signal for workers to stop ranging.
Call close(results) from a goroutine that waits on the WaitGroup so the main range can drain.
bruteForce: Square everything in a single sequential loop. Time Complexity: O(n).
optimized: Fan out to a worker pool and fan in results. Time Complexity: O(n), parallel across workers.

discussion.mistakes: Closing results before workers finish (panic on send) or forgetting to close jobs (workers block forever).
followUps: Propagate the first error from any worker using errgroup.

title: Fan-In Merge of Channels
question: Write `func mergeSorted(chans ...<-chan int) int`. Each input channel emits some integers and is then closed. Concurrently fan in all of them into a single stream using one goroutine per channel and a WaitGroup, and return the total sum of every value received. The result must be deterministic.
solutionCode:
package main

import "sync"

func mergeSorted(chans ...<-chan int) int {
	out := make(chan int)  // merged stream of all values
	var wg sync.WaitGroup  // tracks one forwarding goroutine per input
	wg.Add(len(chans))     // we will start one goroutine per channel
	for _, c := range chans { // fan in each input channel
		go func(in <-chan int) { // capture the loop channel by argument
			defer wg.Done()          // signal this forwarder is finished
			for v := range in {      // drain the input until it is closed
				out <- v         // forward each value to the merged stream
			}
		}(c)
	}
	go func() {        // close the merged stream once all inputs drain
		wg.Wait()  // wait for every forwarder to finish
		close(out) // ends the aggregation range below
	}()
	sum := 0               // accumulate every forwarded value
	for v := range out {   // consume the merged stream
		sum += v // order-independent aggregation
	}
	return sum // total across all input channels
}
hint:
1. Spawn one goroutine per input channel.
2. Each forwards into a shared out channel.
3. Close out after a WaitGroup confirms all drained.
constraints: 0 <= number of channels <= 64. Each producer closes its own channel.
hints: Pass the loop variable as a goroutine argument to avoid capturing the wrong channel.
Closing out exactly once, after wg.Wait, prevents send-on-closed panics.
bruteForce: Drain channels one at a time sequentially. Time Complexity: O(total values), no concurrency.
optimized: Concurrent fan-in with one goroutine per channel. Time Complexity: O(total values).

solutionCode:
package main

import (
	"strconv"
	"strings"
)

type TreeNode struct {
	Val   int          // node value
	Left  *TreeNode    // left child
	Right *TreeNode    // right child
}

func serialize(root *TreeNode) string {
	var sb strings.Builder                       // efficient buffer for building the output
	var pre func(n *TreeNode)                     // recursive preorder helper
	pre = func(n *TreeNode) {                      // define the closure
		if n == nil {                         // nil child -> write a sentinel
			sb.WriteString("#,")          // '#' marks an absent node
			return                        // stop recursing on nil
		}
		sb.WriteString(strconv.Itoa(n.Val))   // write the node value
		sb.WriteByte(',')                     // comma delimiter between tokens
		pre(n.Left)                           // serialize left subtree first (preorder)
		pre(n.Right)                          // then the right subtree
	}
	pre(root)                                     // kick off traversal from the root
	return sb.String()                            // final comma-separated token string
}

func deserialize(data string) *TreeNode {
	tokens := strings.Split(strings.TrimRight(data, ","), ",") // split into tokens, drop trailing comma
	if len(tokens) == 1 && tokens[0] == "" {      // empty input -> empty tree
		return nil                            // nothing to build
	}
	idx := 0                                      // cursor into the token slice
	var build func() *TreeNode                    // recursive rebuilder
	build = func() *TreeNode {                     // define the closure
		tok := tokens[idx]                    // read the current token
		idx++                                 // advance the cursor
		if tok == "#" {                       // sentinel means no node here
			return nil                    // return nil for this position
		}
		val, _ := strconv.Atoi(tok)           // parse the integer value
		n := &TreeNode{Val: val}              // create the node
		n.Left = build()                      // rebuild left subtree (preorder order matches serialize)
		n.Right = build()                     // rebuild right subtree
		return n                              // return the constructed node
	}
	return build()                                // build starting from the root token
}
hint:
1. Preorder: value, then left, then right, using '#' for nil.
2. Deserialize consumes tokens in the same order.
3. Keep a shared index while rebuilding.
constraints: Tree may have up to 10^4 nodes; values fit in int; structure must round-trip exactly.
hints: A nil marker per missing child makes structure unambiguous.
Use a shared cursor variable closed over by the rebuild function.

optimized: Preorder with nil markers and a single linear pass to rebuild. Time Complexity: O(N).

title: Number of Connected Components
question: Write `func countComponents(n int, edges [][]int) int`. Given `n` nodes labeled 0..n-1 and an undirected edge list, return the number of connected components. Use union-find (disjoint set) with path compression and union by rank.
solutionCode:
package main

func countComponents(n int, edges [][]int) int {
	parent := make([]int, n)        // parent[i] is the representative of i's set
	rank := make([]int, n)          // approximate tree height per root, for union by rank
	for i := range parent {         // initialize each node as its own set
		parent[i] = i           // self-parent means a singleton component
	}
	var find func(x int) int        // find-with-path-compression helper
	find = func(x int) int {         // define the closure
		for parent[x] != x {    // walk up until we reach the root
			parent[x] = parent[parent[x]] // path halving: point to grandparent
			x = parent[x]   // move up
		}
		return x                // x is now the root
	}
	count := n                      // start with n separate components
	for _, e := range edges {       // process every edge
		ra, rb := find(e[0]), find(e[1]) // roots of the two endpoints
		if ra == rb {           // already in the same component
			continue        // edge adds no new connection
		}
		if rank[ra] < rank[rb] { // attach the shorter tree under the taller
			ra, rb = rb, ra // ensure ra is the taller root
		}
		parent[rb] = ra         // merge rb's set into ra
		if rank[ra] == rank[rb] { // equal ranks -> resulting tree grows by one
			rank[ra]++      // bump the rank of the new root
		}
		count--                 // two components merged into one
	}
	return count                    // remaining number of components
}
hint:
1. Start with n components.
2. For each edge, union the endpoints if they differ.
3. Each successful union decrements the count.

hints: Path compression keeps find nearly O(1) amortized.

solutionCode:
package main

func findOrder(numCourses int, prerequisites [][]int) []int {
	adj := make([][]int, numCourses)     // adjacency: prereq -> courses that depend on it
	indeg := make([]int, numCourses)     // number of unmet prerequisites per course
	for _, p := range prerequisites {    // p = [a, b]: b must come before a
		adj[p[1]] = append(adj[p[1]], p[0]) // edge b -> a
		indeg[p[0]]++                 // a gains one incoming prerequisite
	}
	queue := []int{}                     // courses with no remaining prerequisites
	for c := 0; c < numCourses; c++ {    // seed the queue
		if indeg[c] == 0 {           // ready to be taken immediately
			queue = append(queue, c)
		}
	}
	order := make([]int, 0, numCourses)  // resulting topological order
	for len(queue) > 0 {                 // process until no ready courses remain
		c := queue[0]                // take the next ready course
		queue = queue[1:]            // dequeue it
		order = append(order, c)     // add to the order
		for _, nxt := range adj[c] { // for each dependent course
			indeg[nxt]--         // one prerequisite satisfied
			if indeg[nxt] == 0 { // now fully unlocked
				queue = append(queue, nxt)
			}
		}
	}
	if len(order) != numCourses {        // some courses never reached zero in-degree
		return []int{}               // a cycle exists -> no valid ordering
	}
	return order                         // a complete valid ordering
}
hint:
1. Compute in-degrees; queue all zero-in-degree courses.
2. Pop a course, append to order, decrement dependents.
3. If the order omits a course, there is a cycle.
constraints: 1 <= numCourses <= 2000; prerequisites have no duplicate edges; return [] on cycle.
hints: Kahn's algorithm naturally detects cycles via leftover nodes.

title: Min Window Substring (sliding)
question: Write `func minWindow(s string, t string) string`. Return the smallest substring of `s` that contains every character of `t` (including multiplicities), or "" if none exists. Use a sliding window with character-frequency counts.
solutionCode:
package main

func minWindow(s string, t string) string {
	if len(s) < len(t) || len(t) == 0 { // window can never cover t -> impossible
		return ""                    // no valid substring
	}
	need := make(map[byte]int)           // required count of each character in t
	for i := 0; i < len(t); i++ {        // tally t's characters
		need[t[i]]++                 // increment required count
	}
	missing := len(t)                    // total characters still needed in the window
	left, start, bestLen := 0, 0, -1     // window left, best start index, best length (-1 = none)
	for right := 0; right < len(s); right++ { // expand the window by moving right
		c := s[right]                // incoming character
		if need[c] > 0 {             // it is a character we still need
			missing--            // one fewer requirement outstanding
		}
		need[c]--                    // record we have one more of c (may go negative)
		for missing == 0 {           // window currently contains all of t
			if bestLen == -1 || right-left+1 < bestLen { // smaller valid window found
				start = left                         // remember its start
				bestLen = right - left + 1           // and its length
			}
			lc := s[left]        // character leaving as we shrink from the left
			need[lc]++           // we no longer have it inside the window
			if need[lc] > 0 {    // it became a required-but-missing character
				missing++    // window no longer valid; stop shrinking
			}
			left++               // advance the left edge
		}
	}
	if bestLen == -1 {                   // never formed a valid window
		return ""                    // no answer
	}
	return s[start : start+bestLen]      // the minimal covering substring
}
hint:
1. Count required chars of t.
2. Expand right; when missing hits 0, try to shrink from the left.
3. Track the smallest valid window seen.
constraints: 1 <= len(s), len(t) <= 10^5; answer is unique if it exists.
hints: Let counts go negative to track surplus characters cleanly.
Only decrement 'missing' when need[c] was still positive.
bruteForce: Check every substring for coverage of t. Time Complexity: O(N^2 * |alphabet|).
optimized: Two-pointer sliding window with frequency counts. Time Complexity: O(N + M).

discussion.whyAsked: The canonical hard sliding-window problem; tests careful expand/contract bookkeeping.
discussion.mistakes: Updating 'missing' on every char instead of only required ones; off-by-one window length.
followUps: Return all minimal windows if there are ties.
Generalize to require a multiset over a large Unicode alphabet.

title: Largest Rectangle in Histogram
question: Write `func largestRectangleArea(heights []int) int`. Given bar heights of equal width 1, return the area of the largest rectangle that fits within the histogram. Use a monotonic increasing stack of bar indices.
solutionCode:
package main

func largestRectangleArea(heights []int) int {
	stack := []int{}             // stack of indices with increasing heights
	best := 0                    // largest rectangle area found
	n := len(heights)            // number of bars
	for i := 0; i <= n; i++ {    // iterate one past the end with a virtual zero-height bar
		cur := 0             // sentinel height for i == n forces the stack to drain
		if i < n {           // real bar height when within bounds
			cur = heights[i]
		}
		for len(stack) > 0 && heights[stack[len(stack)-1]] > cur { // current bar is shorter than stack top
			top := stack[len(stack)-1]      // index of the bar to settle
			stack = stack[:len(stack)-1]    // pop it
			height := heights[top]          // its height bounds the rectangle
			var width int                   // span over which this height extends
			if len(stack) == 0 {            // no shorter bar to the left
				width = i               // rectangle reaches index 0
			} else {                        // bounded on the left by the new stack top
				width = i - stack[len(stack)-1] - 1
			}
			if area := height * width; area > best { // candidate area
				best = area             // update the best
			}
		}
		stack = append(stack, i)         // push the current index (heights now non-decreasing)
	}
	return best                          // maximum rectangle area
}
hint:
1. Keep a stack of indices with non-decreasing heights.
2. When a shorter bar arrives, pop and compute the rectangle bounded by it.
3. Width is current index minus new stack top minus one.
constraints: 1 <= len(heights) <= 10^5; 0 <= heights[i].
hints: Iterate one index past the end with a virtual zero bar to flush the stack.
When the stack empties on a pop, the rectangle extends all the way to index 0.
bruteForce: For each bar, expand left and right while bars are at least as tall. Time Complexity: O(N^2).
optimized: Single pass with a monotonic increasing stack. Time Complexity: O(N).

discussion.whyAsked: The hardest classic monotonic-stack problem; tests width computation on pop.
discussion.mistakes: Wrong width formula after popping; forgetting the trailing sentinel to drain the stack.
followUps: Use it as a subroutine for Maximal Rectangle in a binary matrix.
Compute the area with two passes of nearest-smaller-element arrays.

title: Rate-Limited API Client
question: Write `func processWithRateLimit(items []int, ratePerSec int, work func(int) int) []int`. Process items concurrently but allow at most `ratePerSec` calls to start per second using a token-bucket. Return results in the SAME order as the input items.
solutionCode:
package main

import (
	"sync"
	"time"
)

func processWithRateLimit(items []int, ratePerSec int, work func(int) int) []int {
	results := make([]int, len(items))        // fixed-size output preserves input order by index
	if len(items) == 0 {                      // nothing to do
		return results                    // empty slice
	}
	interval := time.Second / time.Duration(ratePerSec) // spacing between allowed starts
	ticker := time.NewTicker(interval)        // emits a tick every interval
	defer ticker.Stop()                       // release the ticker when done
	var wg sync.WaitGroup                     // wait for all workers to finish
	for i, item := range items {              // index i fixes the result slot
		<-ticker.C                        // block until a token (tick) is available
		wg.Add(1)                         // register one in-flight worker
		go func(idx, val int) {           // capture index and value by value
			defer wg.Done()           // mark this worker complete on return
			results[idx] = work(val)  // write to a unique index -> no data race
		}(i, item)
	}
	wg.Wait()                                 // wait for every worker to finish
	return results                            // results aligned with input order
}

testCases.input: processWithRateLimit([]int{1,2,3}, 100, func(x int) int { return x*x })
processWithRateLimit([]int{5}, 1, func(x int) int { return x+1 })

hint:
1. A time.Ticker emits one token per interval = 1s/ratePerSec.
2. Receive a tick before launching each worker.
3. Write each result to results[i] so order is preserved without a mutex.
constraints: ratePerSec >= 1; each worker writes a distinct index so no lock is needed; use WaitGroup to join.
hints: Writing to disjoint indices of a preallocated slice is race-free.
Receiving from ticker.C throttles the START rate, not the work duration.

title: Channel-Based State Machine
question: Write `func runStateMachine(events []string) []string`. A single goroutine owns the state (idle -> running -> paused/running -> stopped) and receives events ("start","pause","resume","stop") over a channel. It emits the new state after each accepted transition and ignores invalid events. Return the ordered slice of emitted states.
solutionCode:
package main

func runStateMachine(events []string) []string {
	eventCh := make(chan string)   // events flow to the owner goroutine here
	stateCh := make(chan string)   // emitted states flow back to the collector here
	go func() {                    // the single owner of the state variable
		state := "idle"        // initial state
		defer close(stateCh)   // signal completion when all events processed
		for ev := range eventCh { // process each incoming event in order
			next := state  // assume no change unless the transition is valid
			switch {
			case ev == "start" && state == "idle":          // idle -> running
				next = "running"
			case ev == "pause" && state == "running":       // running -> paused
				next = "paused"
			case ev == "resume" && state == "paused":       // paused -> running
				next = "running"
			case ev == "stop" && state != "stopped" && state != "idle": // active -> stopped
				next = "stopped"
			}
			if next != state { // only emit on an accepted transition
				state = next        // commit the new state
				stateCh <- state    // emit it to the collector
			}
		}
	}()
	go func() {                    // feeder goroutine sends events then closes the input
		for _, ev := range events { // push each event in order
			eventCh <- ev
		}
		close(eventCh)         // no more events -> owner will finish
	}()
	var out []string               // collected emitted states
	for s := range stateCh {       // drain emissions until the owner closes stateCh
		out = append(out, s)   // record each new state in order
	}
	return out                     // ordered transitions that actually occurred
}
hint:
1. One goroutine owns the state; communicate via channels.
2. Validate each event against the current state.
3. Emit only on accepted transitions; ignore invalid ones.
constraints: State must be owned by exactly one goroutine (no shared mutation); invalid events are ignored.
hints: "Share memory by communicating": only the owner touches the state variable.
Close the event channel to let the owner close the state channel and end the collector loop.
bruteForce: Mutate a shared state variable from multiple goroutines with a mutex. Time Complexity: O(N) but lock-heavy.
optimized: Single-owner goroutine driven by channels. Time Complexity: O(N).

discussion.mistakes: Sharing the state variable across goroutines; deadlocking by not closing channels.
followUps: Add timeouts that auto-transition running -> paused after inactivity.

title: Throttle with Ticker
question: Write `func throttle(values []int, perTick int, tick time.Duration) [][]int`. Emit the input values in batches of at most `perTick` items, releasing one batch per ticker interval. Return the ordered slice of batches that were emitted.
solutionCode:
package main

import "time"

func throttle(values []int, perTick int, tick time.Duration) [][]int {
	batches := [][]int{}             // ordered batches that get emitted
	if len(values) == 0 || perTick < 1 { // nothing to emit or invalid batch size
		return batches           // return empty result
	}
	ticker := time.NewTicker(tick)   // fires once per interval
	defer ticker.Stop()              // always release the ticker's resources
	i := 0                           // index of the next value to emit
	for i < len(values) {            // keep emitting until all values are released
		<-ticker.C               // wait for the next tick before releasing a batch
		end := i + perTick       // tentative end of this batch
		if end > len(values) {   // clamp to the slice bounds for the final batch
			end = len(values)
		}
		batch := make([]int, end-i) // allocate the batch slice
		copy(batch, values[i:end])  // copy to decouple from the backing array
		batches = append(batches, batch) // record the emitted batch
		i = end                  // advance past the emitted values
	}
	return batches                   // all batches in emission order
}
hint:
1. Create a time.Ticker for the interval.
2. On each tick, slice off up to perTick values.
3. Clamp the final batch and stop when values are exhausted.
constraints: perTick >= 1; release exactly one batch per tick; always Stop() the ticker.
hints: Copy each batch out of the source slice to avoid sharing the backing array.
Clamp the end index so the final partial batch is correct.
bruteForce: Sleep for the interval before slicing each batch. Time Complexity: O(N) wall-clock = (N/perTick)*tick.
optimized: A single ticker gates one batch release per interval. Time Complexity: O(N).

discussion.mistakes: Forgetting ticker.Stop() (leak); sharing the backing array across batches; off-by-one on the last batch.

title: In-Memory Pub/Sub Hub
question: Implement a concurrency-safe in-memory publish/subscribe hub. Define `type Hub struct{...}`, `func NewHub() *Hub`, `func (h *Hub) Subscribe() <-chan string` which returns a new receive-only channel, and `func (h *Hub) Publish(msg string)` which sends the message to every subscriber. Protect the subscriber list with a `sync.Mutex`. Give each subscriber channel a small buffer so a slow subscriber does not block publishing, and use a non-blocking `select` send that drops the message if the buffer is full.
constraints: Concurrency-safe Subscribe/Unsubscribe/Publish. Slow subscribers must not block others.
hints: Keep map[topic][]chan Msg under a mutex.
Publish in a goroutine or use buffered channels + non-blocking send.
Unsubscribe must close and remove the channel.
optimized: Buffered per-subscriber channels with select/default to drop or timeout slow consumers.
bruteForce: Blocking send to each subscriber lets one slow consumer stall the publisher.

discussion.whyAsked: Models the fan-out core of realtime systems and message buses.
discussion.mistakes: Blocking on slow consumers; races on the subscriber map; leaking channels on unsubscribe.
followUps: How would you back this with Redis pub/sub to scale across servers?

title: Cursor Pagination
question: Implement cursor-based pagination over a sorted, ascending slice of ints. Write `func Page(items []int, cursor string, limit int) ([]int, string)`. The `cursor` is an opaque string: an empty cursor means start from the beginning; otherwise it encodes the last id returned so far. Return up to `limit` items whose value is strictly greater than the cursor value, plus a next cursor string (the last returned item's value as a string). When there are no more items, return an empty next cursor. Use `strconv` to decode/encode the cursor. This is how scalable APIs paginate without OFFSET.
exampleOutput: first 2 items + an opaque cursor to fetch the next page
constraints: Cursor encodes the last-seen key; pages are stable under inserts. No offset scanning.
hints: Decode the cursor to a last-seen id (base64 of the key).
Return items after that id, up to limit.
Emit a next cursor from the last returned item (empty if end).
optimized: Keyset (cursor) pagination — O(limit), stable, index-friendly.
bruteForce: OFFSET/LIMIT re-scans skipped rows (O(offset)) and shifts under inserts.

discussion.whyAsked: Cursor pagination is the correct way to page large/real-time datasets.
discussion.mistakes: Leaking internal ids; unstable ordering; not handling deleted cursors.
followUps: How do you paginate a multi-column sort?
Forward vs bidirectional cursors?

title: Retry with Exponential Backoff
question: Implement retry with exponential backoff. Write `func Retry(fn func() error, maxAttempts int, base time.Duration, sleep func(time.Duration)) error`. Call `fn`; if it returns nil, return nil immediately. On error, retry up to `maxAttempts` total calls, sleeping via the injected `sleep` function for a doubling delay (base, 2*base, 4*base, ...) before each retry. Return the last error if all attempts fail. Injecting `sleep` keeps the function deterministically testable (pass a no-op in tests).
exampleOutput: retries up to 3 times with 1s,2s,4s backoff, returns last error
constraints: Exponential backoff (optionally jittered); stop early on success or context cancellation.
hints: Loop attempts; on error, sleep base*2^i.
Respect ctx.Done() between attempts.
Return nil on first success, else the last error.
optimized: Capped exponential backoff with full jitter avoids thundering-herd retries.
bruteForce: Fixed-interval retries synchronize clients and hammer a recovering service.

discussion.whyAsked: Retries are core to resilient service clients.
discussion.mistakes: Retrying non-idempotent ops; no cap/jitter; ignoring context.
followUps: Which errors are safe to retry?
How does this pair with a circuit breaker?

title: Idempotency Key Store
question: Implement an idempotency-key store so repeated operations return the first result. Define `type IdempotencyStore struct{...}`, `func NewIdempotencyStore() *IdempotencyStore`, and `func (s *IdempotencyStore) Do(key string, op func() (string, error)) (string, error)`. If `key` was seen before, return the previously stored result without calling `op` again. Otherwise run `op`, store its result on success, and return it. Guard with a `sync.Mutex`. On error, do not store, so a retry with the same key can succeed. This is how payment APIs prevent double-charging.
exampleOutput: op runs once; second call returns the stored result
constraints: Dedupe by idempotency key; concurrent duplicates must not double-execute.
hints: Store results in map[key]result under a lock.
On a hit, return the stored result without running op.
Use single-flight semantics for concurrent first calls.
optimized: Per-key single-flight + result cache guarantees exactly-once effect per key.
bruteForce: Checking then executing without locking double-runs under concurrency.

discussion.whyAsked: Idempotency keys make payment/webhook/POST retries safe.
discussion.mistakes: TOCTOU race; unbounded key growth (need TTL); caching failures.
followUps: How long do you keep keys?
How does this look with Redis SETNX?

title: Bounded Worker Pool
question: Implement a bounded worker pool. Write `func ProcessJobs(jobs []int, workers int, work func(int) int) []int` that processes every job using at most `workers` goroutines running concurrently and returns a slice of results in the SAME order as the input jobs. Use a jobs channel (feeding indices), a `sync.WaitGroup` to wait for workers, and a pre-sized results slice so each worker writes to its own index (no shared-slot data race). This is the fan-out/fan-in concurrency pattern.
exampleOutput: all jobs processed by ≤4 concurrent workers; results collected
constraints: Bound concurrency to N workers; collect results; no goroutine leaks.
hints: Feed jobs on a channel; start N worker goroutines.
Use sync.WaitGroup to know when all workers finish.
Close the results channel after wg.Wait() in a separate goroutine.
optimized: Fixed worker pool over a jobs channel — bounded memory and concurrency.
bruteForce: Spawning one goroutine per job is unbounded and can exhaust resources.

discussion.whyAsked: Bounded concurrency is the most common Go concurrency interview task.
discussion.mistakes: Deadlock closing channels; leaking workers on early return; unbounded spawn.
followUps: How do you propagate errors/cancellation (errgroup)?

title: Graceful Shutdown Coordinator
question: Implement a graceful shutdown coordinator using context and a WaitGroup. Write `func RunWorkers(ctx context.Context, workers int, step func(id int)) int` that launches `workers` goroutines. Each goroutine loops calling `step(id)` until `ctx` is cancelled (select on `ctx.Done()`), incrementing a shared counter of completed steps (protected against races). When the context is cancelled, all workers must exit cleanly; use a `sync.WaitGroup` to wait for them before returning the total number of steps performed. Use `sync/atomic` or a mutex for the counter.
exampleInput: SIGTERM received while requests in flight
exampleOutput: new work stops; in-flight work drains within a deadline, then exit
constraints: Use context cancellation + sync.WaitGroup; drain within a timeout, then force-exit.
hints: Cancel a root context on signal to stop accepting new work.
WaitGroup tracks in-flight units; Wait() in a goroutine.
select on wg-done vs a timeout to bound the drain.
optimized: Context-driven cancellation + WaitGroup drain with a bounded timeout — graceful and bounded.
bruteForce: os.Exit on signal drops in-flight requests and corrupts partial work.

discussion.whyAsked: Graceful shutdown is required for zero-downtime deploys (k8s SIGTERM).
discussion.mistakes: Not bounding the drain; ignoring SIGTERM; closing resources before drain completes.
followUps: How does this integrate with http.Server.Shutdown?
What is the k8s terminationGracePeriod interplay?
